A.title: Fourth Circuit Backs Maryland Against Kalshi
A.excerpt: A split Fourth Circuit panel refuses Kalshi an injunction against Maryland, deepening the circuit divide over sports event contracts.
body: On 17 November 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit affirmed the August 2025 decision of a Maryland federal district court denying Kalshi a preliminary injunction against the state's gaming regulators. The dispute began in April 2025, when Maryland issued a cease-and-desist letter asserting that Kalshi was offering sports wagering without a Maryland licence. Kalshi responded that its status as a CFTC-designated exchange placed its event contracts under exclusive federal jurisdiction under the Commodity Exchange Act, pre-empting state gambling law. The ruling resolves only the injunction appeal; the underlying lawsuit continues.

The 2-1 decision is notable as much for its reasoning as its result. Judges Roger Gregory and Stephanie Thacker agreed that Kalshi had not shown grounds for an injunction, but they reached that conclusion by different routes. Judge Gregory assumed, without deciding, that sports event contracts are federally regulated swaps, and held that even so Congress had not clearly displaced the states' traditional power to regulate gambling. As he put it, Congress knows how to displace traditional state police powers when it chooses to do so. Judge Thacker went further, concluding that sports event contracts are not swaps under federal commodities law at all and therefore fall outside the CFTC's exclusive jurisdiction.

Judge DeAndrea Benjamin dissented, reasoning that the contracts are swaps and that exclusive jurisdiction belongs to the CFTC. The three opinions neatly capture the three positions now being litigated across the country: that the contracts are not swaps; that they are swaps but state gambling law survives because Congress did not clearly pre-empt it; and that they are swaps and federal jurisdiction is exclusive. The absence of a single majority rationale may limit the decision's precedential force within the circuit, but its practical effect is clear: Maryland may continue to treat unlicensed sports event contracts as illegal wagering while the case proceeds.

The ruling adds to an increasingly lopsided map. The Third Circuit sided with Kalshi against New Jersey in April 2026, but the Ninth Circuit (Nevada, August 2026) and the Sixth Circuit (Ohio and Tennessee, September 2026) have since ruled for the states. New Jersey regulators have petitioned the Supreme Court to review the Third Circuit decision, and prediction market companies have sought review of rulings against them. With the Fourth Circuit now aligned with the majority, the case for certiorari is stronger, but the Court has not yet agreed to hear the dispute and has limited time to do so if a decision is to come this term.

State enforcement is meanwhile accelerating. On 12 November, Judge Jeffrey Johnson of the 21st Judicial District Court in Tangipahoa Parish granted Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill a temporary restraining order, without first hearing the defendants, barring Kalshi, Polymarket and other platforms from offering certain sports, election and awards contracts in Louisiana without state gaming authorisation and requiring geofencing. The CFTC and the United States sued Louisiana in the Eastern District of Louisiana the following day, seeking to block the order on pre-emption grounds and describing it as affecting more than 30 companies. The CFTC has filed a similar action over Arkansas's suit against Kalshi.

For licensed sportsbooks and the prediction market sector, the Fourth Circuit decision matters well beyond Maryland. North Carolina, Virginia and West Virginia, which have regulated sports betting, sit in the same circuit, and their regulators now have appellate support for enforcement. Exchanges, futures commission merchants and clearing members serving customers in those states should reassess their geolocation capabilities and exposure to state penalties, particularly given the CFTC's 5 November interpretation pressing exchanges to remove domestic geographic restrictions. Compliance with one regulator's demand may now place a firm in breach of another's.

Until the Supreme Court acts, operators face a fragmented legal environment in which the lawfulness of the same contract depends on the circuit in which a customer sits. Businesses on both sides of the dispute, including licensed operators considering prediction market partnerships, should document their jurisdictional analysis, monitor the certiorari petitions closely and take specialist advice on federal derivatives and state gaming law before expanding event contract offerings.

A.title: DC Online Casino Bill: 25% Tax, Unlimited Licences
A.excerpt: A DC Council committee has advanced an iGaming bill with a $2m licence fee and a 25% tax. What operators should know before the full vote.
body: Washington, DC moved a step closer to legal online casino gaming on 18 November 2026, when the DC Council's Human Services Committee voted 3-1 to advance legislation introduced in April by Councilmember Wendell Felder. Felder, Matt Frumin and Zachary Parker voted in favour; Christina Henderson voted against. The bill must still pass the full Council, and no timetable has been set. If enacted, the District, with roughly 700,000 residents and no land-based casinos, would become the smallest US jurisdiction to authorise real-money iGaming.

The proposed framework is notably open. Unlike states that tie online casino licences to existing land-based properties, the bill would allow an unlimited number of qualified operators, regulated by the DC Office of Lottery and Gaming (OLG). The application fee would be $2 million, licences would run for five years, and renewal would cost $500,000. Operators could generally use up to two brands, with more permitted with regulatory approval. Authorised games would include online slots, blackjack, roulette and poker.

The economics are less generous. Adjusted gross gaming revenue would be taxed at 25%, with an economic analysis cited at the hearing estimating around $50 million a year in tax receipts. The first $750,000 of annual revenue, increased from $500,000 in the introduced version, would be earmarked for problem gambling prevention and treatment, and a separate 2% community impact assessment could raise about $2 million more. Committee members cited estimates that DC residents wager nearly $1 billion a year on unregulated platforms, the core justification for the bill. Operators will need to weigh a high fixed entry cost and tax rate against a small, though affluent, addressable market.

The bill's consumer protection provisions go further than many existing state regimes. Credit card deposits would be banned, the minimum age would be 21, and advertising would be restricted. Most significantly for compliance design, players under 25 who deposit $500 in a month, and any player whose lifetime deposits reach $2,500, would trigger additional interventions. These are hard-coded, deposit-based thresholds rather than risk-based markers, and operators would need to build monitoring and intervention workflows specific to the District from day one.

Two further obligations will shape operating models. Operators would have to direct at least 35% of their DC-related operating budgets to certified local businesses, subject to waivers, a requirement that affects procurement of marketing, technology and services. A live-dealer requirement could create around 100 union jobs, which implies either a local studio or a partnership with a provider prepared to build one. Both requirements will need careful contractual structuring and early engagement with OLG on how waivers will be assessed.

The timeline, if the bill passes, is aggressive. Regulators would have to open an application process within 30 days of the law taking effect, and online gaming would begin within 180 days unless the mayor determines more preparation is needed, making a 2027 launch possible. Political risk remains: Henderson argued that the District should not build revenue on the backs of people's addictions, and Frumin, while voting in favour, said he would work with her on additional safeguards before later votes. Further amendments, particularly to responsible gambling provisions, are likely.

The DC proposal also sits against a difficult regional backdrop. Virginia's competing iGaming bills failed to reconcile in 2026, and Maryland's proposals did not advance. Only eight states currently authorise real-money online casinos. Operators already licensed for DC sports betting, and suppliers seeking an early foothold, should track the full Council vote, prepare for OLG's application requirements and take advice on the local-spend, live-dealer and intervention obligations before committing to a launch.

A.title: Namibia Suspends New Bookmaker Licence Applications
A.excerpt: Namibia's Gambling Board will refuse new bookmaker and totalisator applications from 30 November and tightens control of machine imports.
body: The Gambling Board of Namibia (GBN) has announced that it will not accept new applications for bookmaker or totalisator licences from 30 November 2026. Public Notice 007 of 2026, published on 17 November and signed by Acting Chief Executive Johannes Erastus, cites an insurmountable number of applications in those two categories. The board says continued submissions are slowing the processing of applications already received, each of which must be evaluated under the Gaming and Entertainment Control Act of 2018. It has not disclosed how many applications are pending or when the window will reopen.

Operators planning Namibian sports betting or pool betting operations should treat 30 November as a hard deadline. Applications not lodged by then will have to wait for the board's decision on future licensing processes, which it has said it will communicate only after it has considered all the applications in hand. For groups that have been preparing submissions, the practical advice is to file a complete application before the cut-off rather than wait to perfect supporting material, provided the application meets the Act's requirements.

Pending applicants also face a stricter process. The notice states that applications will continue through preliminary evaluation and that applicants may be asked for additional, outstanding or updated information. Where an applicant fails or refuses to provide it, the board may stop processing and treat the application as lapsed. Applicants should therefore ensure that corporate, ownership, financial and key-person documentation is current, and should designate someone able to respond quickly to information requests. A lapsed application during a moratorium may leave an operator without a route back into the queue for an indefinite period.

The suspension should be read in the context of the GBN's broader situation. Namibia is in the middle of a gambling law reform process, including consultation on amended regulations and the planned introduction of a central electronic monitoring system, and the board has faced staff shortages that affect its regulatory capacity. A pause on new applications is a pragmatic response to a backlog, but it also suggests that the licensing framework that emerges after reform may differ from the current one. Applicants should be alert to the possibility of new conditions or requirements being applied to applications that are still pending when reforms take effect.

A second notice published the same day, Public Notice 006 of 2026, tightens control over gambling equipment. Gambling machines may only enter or leave Namibia with a letter of approval from the GBN, under a memorandum of understanding signed in March with the Namibia Revenue Agency (NamRA). Requests must be made 14 business days before the intended transport date and must include the manufacturer or supplier, the machine's unique serial number, date of manufacture, purpose of transport, intended transport date and a copy of the relevant gambling licence. The notice does not specify an effective date.

The import and export regime has practical consequences for suppliers and route operators. Shipments that arrive without GBN approval risk being held at the border, and suppliers moving machines between Namibia and neighbouring markets, including South Africa, will need to build the 14-day lead time into logistics and refurbishment cycles. Serial-number-level tracking of equipment also lays the groundwork for the central monitoring system and gives the regulator and customs authority a shared view of machines in circulation. Licence holders should audit their asset registers to ensure that every machine can be documented to the level the notice requires.

Taken together, the two notices show a regulator trying to regain control of its pipeline while reform is under way. Operators and suppliers with Namibian exposure should file outstanding bookmaker or totalisator applications before 30 November, keep pending files up to date, and adjust equipment logistics to the new approval process. Advisers with experience across Southern African gambling regimes can help assess how the moratorium and forthcoming reforms affect market entry plans.

A.title: Guyana Gaming Authority Bill: 30% Remote Tax Explained
A.excerpt: Guyana's gambling overhaul heads to select committee with a 30% remote tax, a G$250m licence fee and a payment-level levy on offshore sites.
body: Guyana's proposed overhaul of its gambling laws has been referred to a special select committee of the National Assembly. Attorney General Anil Nandlall moved the motion on 11 November 2026, and Speaker Manzoor Nadir confirmed that a committee would be established, though its membership and timetable have not yet been announced. The Gaming Authority Bill, first presented in July and published in the Official Gazette on 27 July, would create a new Gaming Authority of Guyana with a remit covering casinos, gaming lounges, betting shops and their agents, online gaming, and betting on broadcast horse and dog races.

The reform would replace the Gaming Authority established in 2008, whose focus was largely on casinos. Its political origins lie in Vice President Bharrat Jagdeo's October 2025 pledge to tighten the law, when he described the spread of local outlets as gambling on demand and a major social problem. The bill therefore combines two objectives that do not always sit easily together: bringing a fragmented retail betting sector under control, and creating a licensed channel for online gambling, which a senior official indicated in August that the government views favourably.

For remote operators, the headline features are the licensing requirement and its cost. No one would be permitted to offer remote gaming to people in Guyana without a licence, and the bill includes a dedicated online gambling licence. Both the application fee and the annual fee are set at G$250 million, roughly US$1.2 million each. For a market of Guyana's size, a recurring seven-figure dollar fee is a significant barrier, and it is likely to limit the field to well-capitalised regional or international groups.

The tax provisions are where the bill is most contentious. Betting shops and gaming lounges would pay 14% of gross bet value, with the same rate applied to prizes or net winnings they pay out. Remote operators would be taxed at 30%. Revenue would be directed to a new Special Responsible Gaming Fund. Operators argue that their objection is to the tax rates, not to regulation as such, warning that a prohibitive regime would cause licensed businesses to fail and push players towards underground or offshore sites. They estimate that more than 5,000 people work directly in the sector, and delivered a petition of around 500 signatures to the president's office in August.

The most novel mechanism is aimed at unlicensed offshore operators. Payment providers would be required to deduct a 30% settlement fee on certain transactions with foreign gaming providers that do not hold a Guyanese licence, covering both payments to those providers and winnings paid from them. Rather than relying on blocking, which is difficult to enforce, the bill would place a collection obligation on the payment chain. For banks, card acquirers and e-money providers, this raises immediate questions about how to identify relevant merchants, how to treat winnings flowing back to customers, and what liability attaches to a failure to deduct.

For offshore operators currently serving Guyanese players under licences from jurisdictions such as Curaçao or Malta, the bill signals the end of a grey-market position. Once enacted, continued service without a local licence would be unlawful, and customer transactions would become materially more expensive through the settlement fee. Operators will need to decide whether the local licence economics justify entry, and if not, plan an orderly exit that protects customer balances.

The select committee stage is the critical window for engagement, as it may recommend amendments before the bill returns to the National Assembly. Operators, suppliers and payment providers should consider making representations on the tax rates, the calculation basis for retail betting, and the scope and mechanics of the settlement fee. Caribbean and international gaming counsel can help prepare submissions and model the impact of the bill's fee and tax structure on market entry decisions.

A.title: Nevada Finalises Gaming Technical Standards Overhaul
A.excerpt: Nevada's revised technical standards take effect 13 December, with compliance required by 1 October 2027. What suppliers must plan for.
body: The Nevada Gaming Control Board (NGCB) has finalised a sweeping revision of its Technical Standards for Gaming Devices and Associated Equipment. Notice 2026-61 to licensees confirms that the revised standards, dated 9 November 2026, take effect on 13 December 2026, while the board has confirmed that the implementation requirement date is 1 October 2027. The standards apply across back-end systems, including slots, keno, payment systems and sportsbooks, so the change touches almost every manufacturer, system supplier and operator in the state.

The project's stated aim is consolidation. Requirements previously spread across multiple sources are now gathered in one place, and several standards had not been updated for years. Of the ten standards in the package, Standards 3, 5 and 6 already existed and have been revised, while Standards 7 to 13 are new. The NGCB's chief of technology, Jeremy Eberwein, said the multi-year project was intended to give stakeholders a resource they can use right away without any interpretation. For compliance teams, that consolidation is welcome, but it also means that familiar requirements may have moved, been renumbered or been restated in ways that change their practical effect.

The process followed the board's usual consultative path. First drafts of the ten standards were posted in September, a workshop was held on 7 October, and second-round comments closed on 15 November. Chair Mike Dreitzer finalised the revisions after considering the comments and recommendations received. Because the final text was settled shortly before the second-round deadline closed, suppliers who submitted late comments should check carefully whether their concerns were addressed and, if not, plan to raise them through ordinary regulatory channels during the implementation period.

The gap between the effective date and the implementation requirement date is the key planning point. The standards are in force from 13 December, but licensees have until 1 October 2027 to bring products and systems into compliance. That window of just under ten months is realistic for most changes but tight for anything requiring re-engineering, independent test laboratory work and NGCB approval. Manufacturers should assume that laboratory and approval queues will lengthen as the deadline approaches and should front-load submissions for higher-risk products.

A structured gap analysis is the sensible first step. Suppliers should map each existing product and system against the revised Standards 3, 5 and 6 and the new Standards 7 to 13, identify which requirements are new rather than merely restated, and determine which products will be retired rather than updated. Operators should obtain written compliance roadmaps from their suppliers, particularly for sportsbook and payment systems, and build contractual protections against non-compliance at the October 2027 deadline into renewals and new procurements.

There is also a governance dimension. Governor-elect Aaron Ford takes office in January, and the terms of Chair Dreitzer and board member George Assad expire on 29 January 2027. Ford may reappoint them or make new appointments; his office has not indicated a decision, and Dreitzer has said he would welcome a full term. A change in board leadership is unlikely to unwind finalised standards, but it could affect the board's approach to interpretation, waivers and enforcement priorities during the implementation period, including its work on supplier standards and anti-money laundering.

Because Nevada's standards are widely referenced by other regulators and test laboratories, the revisions may influence product requirements beyond the state. Suppliers with multi-jurisdiction portfolios should consider whether to adopt the Nevada changes as a baseline across their products. Specialist gaming regulatory counsel in Nevada can help licensees interpret the new standards, plan approval submissions and engage with the NGCB on any implementation issues before the 1 October 2027 deadline.
